name: C shell
title: C shell (csh 8.2 / tcsh)

presenceList.meta: R1, Ec1, Ec3, G1, G2, G3, Q2

type.text: **Every value is a word list**: `set` binds a list of words to a name, and no declaration states what the name holds, so the same variable carries a path on one line and a number on the next
**No sum types**: An option that may be absent, numeric, or textual is one string, and the reader must decode the convention (`set flag` versus `set flag=0`) to tell them apart
**No generics**: A command is specialised only by the words passed to it, so the same logic is written again for each shape of data

**Arithmetic is a second grammar**: `@` and `if ( expr )` evaluate C operators over words, so a number is a word that is re-parsed at each use, a null or missing argument counts as `0`, and a non-numeric word raises `Badly formed number`
**One flat namespace**: `set` variables and `setenv` environment variables form two flat spaces with no lexical scope, so a `source`d file cannot hide a name from its caller (T6, T11)
**An unset name expands to empty**: Csh has no `nounset` option — its letters are `-bcefimnstVvXx` — so a misspelled variable becomes an empty argument instead of an error

construction.text: **No function scope**: A variable set in a script is visible to every command the script runs, and a `source`d file writes directly into the caller's namespace
**No immutability by default**: Every name is writable everywhere, so a value read at the top of a script can change before it is used
**Aliases are the only reuse mechanism**: An `alias` is textually substituted with `\!*` arguments, so its body is expanded in the caller's context instead of a protected one
**Recursion re-enters the script**: With no function call, a recursive routine re-invokes `$0`, which couples the logic to the script path and to the positional parameters
**tcsh can freeze a variable**: `set -r` marks a name read-only, but this is a tcsh extension and it is never the default
**`path` is tied to `PATH`**: Assigning the `path` word list re-exports `PATH`, so the search path is edited as a list rather than by string editing

memory.text: **No allocation syntax**: The language has no pointer, no address, and no `free`, so word lists are allocated by the interpreter on assignment
**No deallocation to manage**: `unset` drops a name and the interpreter reclaims the words, so a script has no free order and no double free to avoid
**Assignment copies the list**: `set b = ($a)` duplicates every word, so a large list is held twice while the assignment runs
**Global scope extends lifetime**: Because every variable is global, data created early in a session stays resident until it is explicitly `unset`
**Word lists are the only aggregate**: There are no user-visible buffers or arenas, so memory layout never enters a script

error.text: **No structured error path**: Csh gives `onintr` for interrupts and `$status` for the last exit code, but there is no exception, no error value, and no handler that can return a result
**`$status` is lost by the next command**: Any command resets it, so a test placed between a failure and its check silently discards the error
**Errors do not compose**: A failure is a global word rather than a value that can be returned, combined, or stored, so recovery cannot be factored into a routine
**Diagnostics are short and late**: The parser is ad hoc, so a fault such as `0: Event not found.` reaches the user only when the line runs and names nothing beyond the command
**The parser reads a command at a time**: A syntax error later in a file is reported when execution reaches it, so earlier side effects are already committed
**`onintr` couples cleanup to a label**: The handler is a named target in the script rather than a scope, so cleanup cannot be attached to the thing it cleans up

concurrency.text: **No concurrency primitives**: `&` and job control start and steer jobs, but there is no lock, channel, or await, so coordination is done by signals and exit codes
**Processes are the unit of parallelism**: The language models concurrency as separate processes joined by pipes, so no shared address space has to be reasoned about
**Job control isolates the terminal**: Csh introduced job control, so a foreground or background decision does not require the script to manage the terminal itself
**`wait` is the only join**: `wait` blocks for all jobs or one named job and returns no value, so a result must travel through a file or a pipeline
**Background jobs inherit the whole environment**: A `&` job shares every global variable and the current directory, so ordering between jobs is unspecified unless the script waits
**No coprocess**: Unlike ksh's `|&`, csh offers no supported two-way conversation with a child, so a pipeline stage cannot be driven interactively

platform.text: **Two implementations of one lineage**: The language is defined by the frozen BSD `csh` 8.2 and by `tcsh`, so there is no third implementation to check behaviour against
**The frozen and maintained dialects differ**: `set -r`, `bindkey`, and the completion system are tcsh additions, so a script that uses them is not a csh script
**No standard to be portable to**: The POSIX committee chose KornShell, so csh has no specification and its contracts live in two manuals
**tcsh is packaged nearly everywhere**: Tcsh ships on the BSDs, Linux, and macOS, where `csh` normally resolves to tcsh, so an interpreter is usually present
**Interactive configuration transfers within the family**: `alias`, `history`, `!!`, tilde expansion, and the directory stack behave the same in csh and tcsh
**Scripting support is frozen**: New portable automation targets other shells, so csh is maintained rather than extended

performance.text: **Interpreted with no compilation step**: Every command line is parsed and evaluated as text at run time, so a loop over files pays parser cost per iteration
**Builtins are a short list**: `cd`, `set`, `@`, and `echo` avoid a process, and almost everything else forks and executes
**Path hashing avoids repeated search**: `rehash` and `hashstat` keep a table of resolved command paths, so command lookup does not rescan `PATH`
**Scripts start without interactive configuration**: Tcsh reads `.tcshrc` for interactive shells only, so a script pays no start-up cost for prompt and completion setup
**Arithmetic is re-parsed per evaluation**: `@` evaluates its expression each time it runs, so a numeric loop is far slower than compiled code
**The shell is rarely the bottleneck**: Time goes to the external commands it spawns, so interpreter overhead matters mainly in arithmetic-heavy loops

ecosystem.text: **No package manager**: There is no distribution channel for csh code, so shared routines are copied between scripts or vendored as files
**The user base is small and narrowing**: Csh survives as a login-shell option on the BSDs and macOS, and new scripting rarely targets it
**Documentation is complete and stable**: The csh and tcsh manuals describe the language fully and have changed little in decades
**Interactive tooling is mature in tcsh**: `bindkey`, `complete`, and the `set` toggles are documented and widely configured
**No static analysis**: ShellCheck does not analyse csh or tcsh, so a csh script has no mainstream linter
**Scripts are the interchange format**: `csh` is invoked from `make`, `cron`, and login configuration without a binding layer

evolution.text: **Backward compatibility is total**: Tcsh runs csh scripts unchanged and adds behaviour through new builtins and `set` variables
**No version treadmill**: No breaking change can arrive for frozen csh, and decades-old scripts still run
**Fixes arrive only in tcsh**: A defect or an unhelpful message in csh stays, and the remedy is to install tcsh and let `csh` point at it
**Two dialects share one manual**: The tcsh manual marks tcsh-only behaviour with `(+)`, so a reader must know which shell they have
**No standardisation track**: With POSIX committed to KornShell, no committee can modernise the language

domain.text: **Adequate as an interactive login shell**: History, aliases, tilde notation, the directory stack, and job control cover terminal work
**Weak as a scripting language**: `foreach`, `while`, `if`, and `switch` cannot be piped into one another, so a data-processing script must be rebuilt around that limit
**Text handling calls out to other tools**: There are no associative arrays and no substring operators beyond the `:r`, `:e`, `:h`, and `:t` modifiers, so `sed` and `awk` do the work
**Arithmetic is integer only in csh**: `@` and `expr` cover integers, so floating-point calculation leaves the shell
**Configuration files are the native domain**: `.cshrc`, `.login`, and `.logout` express an interactive environment directly
**Legacy maintenance persists**: Csh remains a login shell on some BSD and macOS accounts, so its configuration files still need care

learning.text: **The interactive surface is gentle**: History substitution, aliases, and tilde notation are learnable in an afternoon
**The grammar resembles C**: `if ( $#argv > 1 )` and `@` arithmetic read as expected to a C programmer
**The scripting limits are learned by failure**: A beginner discovers that a control structure cannot be piped only when the pipeline fails
**Word modifiers must be memorised**: `:r`, `:e`, `:h`, `:t`, `:g`, and `:q` are a compact but unguessable syntax for path and quoting work
**`set` and `setenv` confuse newcomers**: Two binding commands with different rules produce silent mistakes when the wrong one is used

syntax.text: **Block terminators disagree**: `if` closes with `endif`, `switch` with `endsw`, and `foreach` and `while` with `end`
**`set`, `setenv`, and `alias` follow different rules**: Three ways to bind a name use three argument conventions
**No separate stderr redirection**: `>&` merges the two streams and `|&` pipes both, so a stream cannot be redirected on its own
**Terse for its work**: `foreach f (*.c)` with `if (-e $f)` expresses a loop and a test in a few characters
**Word modifiers are short and local**: `$file:r.c` and `$path:h` perform path surgery inline
**`@` and `if ( expr )` add a second reading of a line**: The same word is a string in one place and an expression in another

testing.text: **No test framework in the language**: A test is a script that calls the code and compares `$status`, with no assertion, fixture, or reporting facility
**Debugging is `echo` and `set -x`**: Csh prints commands with `set echo` and the `-x` option, but has no breakpoint, no state inspection, and no debugger
**Faults appear only in the branch that runs**: With no static check, a mistyped variable or a bad `foreach` pattern is found during the test run
**A hand-built harness is possible**: `$status` and `onintr` allow a script to record an outcome and report it
**Exit status is a usable oracle**: After a command, `if ($status == 0)` tests the one outcome the language reports reliably
**Interactive behaviour needs a terminal**: History, completion, and prompt behaviour are tty-driven, so they resist automated checks

security.text: **Unquoted expansion is re-parsed**: Because a value is a word list, an unquoted `$var` splits and globs, so untrusted text can change the number of arguments a command receives
**`eval` and `$<` feed outside text to the parser**: Both re-enter the interpreter with text that is not validated
**No restricted mode**: Csh offers no sandbox and no capability model, so a script's protection is the file permissions of its user
**`set noclobber` protects existing files**: The option makes `>` refuse to overwrite, so a mistake cannot silently destroy data
**Environment changes are explicit**: `setenv` and `unsetenv` are named builtins, so a script's effect on its children is visible in the text
**No memory-safety surface**: There are no pointers and no manual allocation, so memory defects belong to the programs csh runs

tradeoffs: **Interactive first, scriptable second**: The design targets the terminal, so a weak scripting surface is a priority choice rather than a defect in the language
**The C-like expression grammar is a deliberate borrowing**: `@` and `if ( expr )` give a C programmer a familiar evaluation model; the cost is a second grammar, not a forced dependency
**The 1993 freeze is a maintenance decision**: Original csh is complete and unmaintained while tcsh continues the line, so the freeze is a project decision rather than a coupling mechanism
**`set` and `setenv` are two commands by history**: The split mirrors the shell-variable and environment-variable distinction that every shell must represent somehow
**The ad-hoc parser is one implementation's shortcut**: A different implementation could parse the same language properly, so the parser defect is not part of the language contract
**csh is not a general-purpose language**: An interpreter plus a set of external commands is the assumed platform, which is a scope decision
verdict: The C shell gives the coupling profile of a word-based shell: values are words, names have one global scope, and an error is a global status word rather than a composable value, which keeps the core score low. Its own contributions are interactive — history, aliases, tilde notation, the directory stack, job control, and path hashing — and none of them separates concerns inside a script. The original shell has been frozen since 1993 and tcsh carries the line forward, so the language is stable but small, and tcsh-only extensions such as `set -r` and the completion system sit outside what a csh script may rely on.

energy.text: Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.

ai-readiness.text: Moderate training data: models write it competently, with measurable language-specific weakness [@joel2025lowresource].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: The installed interpreter reads the source at run time; no compiled unit crosses a boundary
